contextTopics.label: Russlands Krieg gegen die Ukraine
background: Russland überfiel die Ukraine am 24. Februar 2022 in vollem Umfang. Vorausgegangen war die Annexion der Krim im März 2014 und der von Russland unterstützte bewaffnete Konflikt im Donbas ab April 2014.

Die UN-Generalversammlung verurteilte den Angriff am 2. März 2022 mit 141 zu 5 Stimmen und forderte den sofortigen Rückzug. Die EU, die USA und weitere Staaten verhängten seither mehrere Sanktionspakete.
Der Internationale Strafgerichtshof erließ im März 2023 einen Haftbefehl gegen Wladimir Putin wegen der Verschleppung ukrainischer Kinder.
Österreich ist militärisch neutral, beteiligt sich aber an den EU-Sanktionen und leistet humanitäre Hilfe. Waffenlieferungen erfolgen nicht.

contextTopics.label: Krieg in Gaza und im Nahen Osten
background: Die Hamas verübte am 7. Oktober 2023 einen Großangriff auf Israel mit rund 1.200 Toten und etwa 250 Verschleppten. Israel begann daraufhin eine großangelegte Militäroperation im Gazastreifen.
Der Konflikt reicht weit zurück: Israel wurde 1948 gegründet, es folgten mehrere Kriege mit arabischen Nachbarstaaten. Der Gazastreifen wird seit 2007 von der Hamas kontrolliert.
Der Internationale Gerichtshof befasst sich seit Dezember 2023 mit einer Klage Südafrikas wegen mutmaßlichen Völkermords; ein Urteil in der Hauptsache steht aus.

Zahlenangaben zu Opfern stammen je nach Meldung von unterschiedlichen Stellen — der von der Hamas geführten Gesundheitsbehörde, israelischen Angaben oder UN-Organisationen. Sie sind selten unabhängig überprüfbar.

contextTopics.label: Handelskonflikte und Zölle
background: Die USA erhoben ab 2018 unter Präsident Trump Zölle auf Stahl, Aluminium und zahlreiche chinesische Waren. China antwortete mit Gegenzöllen. Teile davon blieben auch unter der Nachfolgeregierung bestehen.
Die EU ist als Zollunion für die Handelspolitik ihrer Mitgliedsstaaten zuständig — Österreich verhandelt also nicht selbst, sondern die Europäische Kommission.
Zölle wirken auf zwei Wegen: Sie verteuern eingeführte Waren für Verbraucher im Einfuhrland und treffen Exporteure im Ausland. Wer die Kosten trägt, ist wirtschaftswissenschaftlich umstritten.

contextTopics.label: Inflation und Zinspolitik der EZB
background: Die Europäische Zentralbank hat als vorrangiges Ziel Preisstabilität, definiert als 2 Prozent Inflation mittelfristig. Sie steuert darüber den Leitzins für den gesamten Euroraum.
Nach Jahren mit Null- und Negativzinsen begann die EZB im Juli 2022 mit Zinserhöhungen, um die stark gestiegene Inflation zu dämpfen — ausgelöst unter anderem durch Energiepreise und Lieferengpässe.

Österreich lag bei der Inflationsrate über Jahre über dem Euroraum-Durchschnitt. Die Gründe dafür sind umstritten; genannt werden unter anderem Energiepreise, Mietanpassungen und der Gastronomiesektor.

contextTopics.label: Klimapolitik und Klimaziele
background: Im Pariser Abkommen von 2015 verpflichteten sich fast alle Staaten, die Erderwärmung deutlich unter 2 Grad gegenüber dem vorindustriellen Niveau zu halten und 1,5 Grad anzustreben.
Die EU hat sich auf Klimaneutralität bis 2050 festgelegt und Zwischenziele für 2030 beschlossen. Österreich strebt Klimaneutralität bis 2040 an — früher als die EU-Vorgabe.

Der Weltklimarat IPCC fasst regelmäßig den Forschungsstand zusammen. Dass die Erwärmung überwiegend menschengemacht ist, gilt dort als gesichert; umstritten sind Tempo, regionale Folgen und Gegenmaßnahmen.

contextTopics.label: Regulierung künstlicher Intelligenz
background: Die Europäische Kommission legte 2021 den Entwurf für den AI Act vor, die weltweit erste umfassende Regulierung künstlicher Intelligenz. Er stuft Anwendungen nach Risiko ein und verbietet einige ganz.
Das Gesetz gilt für Anbieter, die ihre Systeme im EU-Markt anbieten — unabhängig davon, wo sie sitzen. Die Pflichten greifen gestaffelt über mehrere Jahre.
Kritik kommt von zwei Seiten: Teilen der Industrie, die Wettbewerbsnachteile befürchten, und Bürgerrechtsorganisationen, denen die Ausnahmen für Sicherheitsbehörden zu weit gehen.

contextTopics.label: Österreichische Innenpolitik
background: Österreich ist eine parlamentarische Demokratie. Der Nationalrat mit 183 Abgeordneten wird alle fünf Jahre gewählt; die Regierung braucht dessen Vertrauen.
Der Bundespräsident wird direkt gewählt, ernennt die Regierung und kann sie entlassen — eine Befugnis, die historisch selten genutzt wurde.
Untersuchungsausschüsse sind ein Minderheitsrecht: Ein Viertel der Abgeordneten kann einen einsetzen, ohne Zustimmung der Mehrheit.

contextTopics.label: Raiffeisen Bank International
background: Die Raiffeisen Bank International (RBI) ist eine der größten Banken Österreichs mit Schwerpunkt in Zentral- und Osteuropa. Sie ging 2010 aus der Fusion von RZB-Teilen und Raiffeisen International hervor.
Der Raiffeisen-Sektor ist genossenschaftlich aufgebaut: lokale Raiffeisenbanken, darüber Landesbanken, darüber die RBI. Diese Struktur erklärt, warum Entscheidungen oft mehrere Ebenen betreffen.
Das Russland-Geschäft der RBI steht seit dem Angriff auf die Ukraine unter besonderer Beobachtung von EZB und US-Behörden. Ein Rückzug wurde mehrfach angekündigt und verzögerte sich.

items.title: A Painful Modernization Story
items.summary: Image Leadership at one company wanted to modernize their core platform. There was an obvious way to do it. They chose the other way. After years of investment, the modernization had delivered nothing, millions had gone to consultants, and the company was downsizing. What went wrong? The obvious way This is not a unique story. A lot of companies overcomplicate their modernizations. At this company, they already had a high-performing Scrum Team managing their core product. The obvious move was to engage their existing Product Owner and empower them to lead the modernization effort with the current Scrum Team. They already understood the business, the customers, the edge cases, and the real constraints. They had the empirical knowledge that only comes from delivering value Sprint after Sprint, and they'd just wrapped up a major initiative successfully. Done right, this was a chance to energize the team that already knew the product best. They could have started replacing the existing system a piece at a time and learning as they went. If leadership wanted to move faster, they could have added additional staff and support to the existing Scrum Team. The other way Instead of engaging their existing Scrum Team, the company formed several new Scrum Teams to do the modernization effort. Leadership then decided that because the new Scrum Teams were just rebuilding the current product, they didn't need a Product Owner . They worked for six months without a Product Owner, but nothing usable was delivered. When the organization finally did add Product Owners, they weren't really empowered to make real business decisions. It was too little, too late. Here's what went wrong: Siloed teams . Not only were they separated from the current team, but the new teams were formed around technology silos which created unnecessary dependencies. No empowered Product Owner . No one was empowered to steer the modernization effort. Big-bang thinking . Unrealistic, leadership-defined deadlines, no incremental delivery. Ignoring the people closest to the work. Money and Vice Presidents instead of engaging the team that already knew the product. No Empirical approach. They didn't adjust their delivery approach beyond just surface-level changes when things weren't going well. Development and testing were in separate Sprints. They hired a design firm who put together a front-end design and html in one Sprint, and then back-end development and testing was done in the following Sprint. Repeatedly what was delivered couldn't be used and had to be sent back which caused delays on top of delays. I have watched versions of this story play out before, and throwing more money at it is not the answer and siloed teams rarely work well. The result of getting the structure wrong Ignoring existing institutional knowledge and starting over with a group that had no empowered Product Owner was not “saving money.” It was the most expensive decision they could have made. In the end, the company wasted so much money that it led to downsizing. They never got their modernization. Instead, they got restructured. How to get it right Great modernization efforts don't happen by accident. They start with the right structure and the right people already in place. Start with good structure First off, a Product Owner is not optional. A Product Owner owns the Product Goal, orders the backlog, and makes strategic decisions. Without an empowered Product Owner, a Scrum Team is just a group of people throwing code around. Energize your high-performing teams Leadership should not redesign the org chart every time they get excited about a new technology. Leadership should remove impediments, make sure the team has the resources they need, and make sure the team is working together effectively. Keep the high-performing teams. Give them the support they need. If the old system truly needs to be replaced, the people who already understand the volume, the data, and the business rules are the ones best positioned to make that transition safely and incrementally. Plan for Incremental Delivery A year of work with nothing usable to show for it is not Agile. Modernization doesn't have to mean a big-bang rewrite. Encourage the Scrum Team to break the work down. They should deliver small, usable pieces of the new system, get feedback, and build on it. Let the team plan their own Sprints instead of chasing top-down deadlines set before anyone understood the scope of the work. Three questions to ask before you modernize If your organization is about to launch a modernization effort, ask yourself three questions. Who has organizational knowledge - Who already owns the current Product and has the deepest knowledge of it? Is the team structured for success? - Are we organizing around the Product or around technology silos? Can we allow them to self-organize? Are we planning for incremental delivery? - Will we deliver usable increments every Sprint, or are we planning a multi-year rewrite…

items.title: The Product Goal Nobody Uses
items.summary: Image In Professional Scrum Product Owner training, I ask every class the same question on the second day: describe your Product Goal. Almost everyone can answer. Most have one written down somewhere, on a slide or in a Confluence page, and the room moves on quickly. Then I ask a second question: which items in your current backlog would you remove because they do not contribute to that goal? That question takes longer. The 2020 Scrum Guide added the Product Goal as the commitment for the Product Backlog [1]. Before that revision, teams were expected to have a product direction, but Scrum never formalized it or tied it to the backlog. The 2020 update made the goal a first-class artifact commitment, alongside the Sprint Goal and the Definition of Done. The Scrum Guide describes the rest of the backlog as emerging "to define what will fulfill the Product Goal" [1]. The backlog is supposed to grow from the goal. Most teams fill the backlog first and write the goal second. The Backlog-First Problem Teams with an existing backlog and a new Product Goal write a goal that fits what they already have. They have no real choice: the backlog contains years of stakeholder requests, technical debt, customer feedback, and executive priorities. Any goal specific enough to exclude some of those would immediately surface conflicts nobody has resolved. So the goal ends up broad enough to cover everything, because it was shaped to match. Stefan Wolpers calls this "retroactively squeezed under a made-up Product Goal" and names it cargo-cult Scrum [2]. The practices are present, but the logic that gives them meaning is gone. Writing the goal to fit the backlog reverses the relationship the Guide describes: the backlog is supposed to flow from the goal, not precede it. When a new request arrives, the question should be: does this advance toward the Product Goal? Teams with a retroactive goal cannot answer that honestly. The goal was built to cover everything in the backlog. Why Sprint Goals Lose Direction The Product Goal and Sprint Goal are supposed to cascade. The Scrum Guide says Sprints "enable predictability by ensuring inspection and adaptation of progress toward a Product Goal" [1]. Sprint Planning checks how selected items "map to the Product Goal" [1]. Each Sprint Goal is a planned step toward the Product Goal. Without a real Product Goal, Sprint Goals describe what will ship this Sprint. The connection to any larger direction gets lost. Teams commit to shipping features with no connection to where the product is supposed to end up. This shows up in Sprint Reviews: teams present what was built, stakeholders check things off, and nobody asks how the Sprint contributed to the Product Goal. The Scrum Guide Expansion Pack names this gap in the artifact itself [3]. Output done means the increment was built. Outcome done is the harder test: whether the business goal was reached. A team without a functioning Product Goal can only say whether the increment was built. The connection between Sprint Goal and Product Goal breaks down quietly. No single Sprint feels misaligned. Over time the product drifts, built sprint by sprint toward nowhere in particular. The Fulfill-or-Abandon Constraint The Scrum Guide requires the team to "fulfill (or abandon) one objective before taking on the next" [1], a constraint that rarely comes up in Sprint Planning. A specific Product Goal lets the team eventually confirm whether they reached it, or decided not to pursue it. A vague goal broad enough to cover the whole backlog can never be fulfilled, and without a clear destination, progress cannot be measured. It never gets inspected at a Sprint Review, because there is nothing concrete enough to check against. Writing a Product Goal commits the team to eventually answering whether the product did what they set out to do. Without that commitment, the team builds indefinitely and never decides whether they arrived. The harder case is the established product with no natural end point. A SaaS platform running for a decade cannot "fulfill" a goal like "be the most reliable tool in the market." That objection is fair, but narrowing the scope solves it: not "be the most reliable" but something measurable in a defined period. The Product Goal names the next destination. The fulfill-or-abandon language exists because the goal is supposed to be finite, not because every product has a built-in expiry date. Three Questions A Product Goal doing its job makes the backlog smaller. Items either advance toward it or they do not. The first question is the most important: can the Scrum Team use it to reject a backlog item? If the goal is specific enough to say no to something, it is filtering. If every item qualifies, the goal has no filtering function. Most teams, when pressed, cannot reject anything using theirs. Does the most recent Sprint Goal connect to it? The Scrum Guide says Sprint Planning should check how items "map to the Product Goal" [1]. A Sprint Goal…

items.title: We’re Not Paid to Practice Scrum, but Answer 5 Product Questions
items.summary: TL;DR: Five Product Questions Cheap Code Makes More Expensive to Skip For decades, the cost of building software rationed what an organization could start: nobody could afford to build everything, so somebody had to choose, however crudely. AI has weakened that rationing; the frontier labs need your organization to use more AI with every model generation, and the product operating model promises to fix what Agile supposedly broke. None of this guarantees that anyone asks whether the work solves a customer problem, nor whether solving it was worth the cost. You need to address these product questions yourself. These product questions become more expensive to skip when starting work gets cheap: which problem is worth solving, whether the work is the best use of the team’s time, whether it is good enough for the people who will see it, whether it solved the problem, and whether the team’s way of working still fits. AI agents can prepare evidence under the A3 Framework’s Assist category, where the agent analyzes and people decide, while explicit standards for AI-assisted work, such as the AI Definition of Done, and recurring inspections, such as the AI Delegation Audit, keep the answers honest. Whether you call any of this Scrum is the least interesting question of all. Image Thesis : This article explains five product questions that become more consequential when AI makes software implementation cheap, why falling AI costs increase the volume of work those questions must filter, and how teams set working principles during early AI adoption. Disclaimer : I read Charniak/McDermott’s book on “Artificial Intelligence” decades ago; of course, I use AI for research, translations, proofreading, challenging story arcs and article structures, creating artifacts such as graphics, and summarization. It is a production tool, not a substitute for thinking. If We’re Not Paid to Practice Scrum, What Are We Paid For? If you work in product, you probably believe that the slow, expensive build was the big problem of software development and that AI coding agents are finally solving it. Half of that belief holds up: building was slow and expensive, and agents have made writing code much cheaper. The other half deserves more scrutiny, because the expense was doing a crude rationing job that many organizations never replaced with anything better. When a feature took a team several weeks, somebody had to decide which idea got those weeks, and some weak ideas died in a prioritization meeting before anyone wrote a line of code. (Not many, admittedly; the ones with a senior sponsor and budget authority usually survived, and being chosen said nothing about whether an idea addressed a worthwhile problem.) The same expense also did damage, discouraging cheap experiments and pushing organizations to defend features they had already paid for in a prime example of submitting to the sunk cost fallacy. Product management has a name for the discipline that rationing never supplied on its own, and Uri Levine, the co-founder of Waze, put it into the title of his 2023 book, Fall in Love with the Problem, Not the Solution . When writing code costs next to nothing, falling in love with your own solution becomes affordable again. At the same time, testing whether customers care becomes cheaper than ever. For years, I have used one sentence to describe what agile practitioners are actually paid for: We are not paid to practice Scrum but to solve our customers’ problems within the given constraints while contributing to the organization’s sustainability. That sentence seems more useful now than ever, as Agile in general and Scrum in particular are under pressure from two sides at once. Two Promises of Speed, and What Adoption Does Not Guarantee The first pressure comes from the product operating model Marty Cagan popularized. He made the point plainly when I interviewed him in 2024: “To be blunt, a Scrum team is quite amateur compared to a professional product team,” as he put it in our interview on the product operating model and Scrum’s future . On paper, the model covers the questions this article is about. SVPG’s introduction to the product operating model states that “leaders in product management, technology, and design are responsible for deciding which problems to solve,” and it asks teams to find solutions that are valuable, usable, feasible, and viable. Adoption is a different matter. In my August 2026 survey of 48 practitioners , only 1 of the 26 respondents whose organizations had adopted the model or were moving toward it reported “a fundamental change in how build decisions are made.” Of the others, 9 described mostly relabeling, 9 a mix of real change and relabeling, and 7 said it was too early to tell. The respondents report on their organizations, though, and the survey did not verify 26 distinct organizations. Putting the model’s vocabulary on the slides seems to be easy, whereas changing who decides what to build, and on which…

items.title: Beyond the Dam of Knowledge Hoarding
items.summary: Picture a developer. Let's call him Chris. Chris has been with the company for twelve years. He knows the billing module better than anyone. When something breaks there, everyone calls him. Documentation? Barely any. Pair programming? Not really his thing. Chris isn't a bad guy. Chris has simply learned how to survive in organizations. If you know something nobody else knows, you're needed. If you're needed, you're safe. For decades, that worked, until AI arrived. It reads the billing module in seconds. It explains to anyone on the team what Chris spent twelve years learning. It finds the bug that used to require a call to Chris. To Chris, this feels like a break-in. As if someone forced open the door to his safe room. What do people do when they feel threatened? They build the walls higher. Chris avoids the AI tools. He finds reasons why they won't work on "his" code. He holds on to his knowledge even tighter. Research has a name for this pattern: knowledge hiding. And it shows that people who hide knowledge end up hurting their own creativity the most. For Scrum Masters, one finding matters most. This effect gets stronger in a performance-driven climate and weaker in a climate focused on learning, mastery and collaboration. So the team climate makes a difference. And shaping that climate is our job. The Scrum Guide describes Scrum Masters as true leaders who serve the Scrum Team and the wider organization. Your job is not to convince Chris. And certainly not to expose him. Your job is to create a space where the dam is no longer necessary. That takes qualities often dismissed as "soft." Empathy. Listening. Sensing what goes unsaid in the team. These qualities are now becoming the core of the role. Because behind hoarded knowledge there is almost always a question nobody asks out loud: What am I still needed for when my knowledge is no longer special? Here is what you can do. Name the fear without judging it. In the Sprint Retrospective, in a one-on-one. "I notice AI is making some of us uneasy. I feel it too." That sentence opens more doors than any tool training. Tell a new story about value. Chris was never valuable because he memorized code. He was valuable because he understands why the system was built this way. What problems it solves. Where the traps are. AI can't replace that judgment. It needs it. Make learning visible and small. No big rollout. One pairing slot per Sprint where Chris works on his module with AI, together with a junior colleague. He brings the why, the AI brings the how, the colleague brings the questions. Celebrate sharing, not knowing. Change what gets recognized. Not "Who solved the hardest problem?" but "Who made sure the team can now solve it on their own?" Lead by not knowing. Say it openly: "I'm learning this too." When you let yourself be seen learning, your team can do the same. That's the Scrum value of openness in action. Knowledge that is held back builds up. It gets heavy. Eventually it seeps away. Knowledge that flows carries the whole team. AI doesn't take Chris's place. It takes away the dam he had to hide behind. What remains is what he is truly needed for. Our job as Scrum Masters is to walk with him to get there. Not in front of him. Beside him. How do you see this in your teams? Is there a Chris on yours?

items.title: A Ilusão da Eficiência Sintética: Por Que a IA Pode Criar a Fábrica de Features Mais Rápida da História
items.summary: Image A inteligência artificial generativa removeu o atrito mecânico da gestão de produtos. Com um único comando estruturado, qualquer profissional consegue desdobrar uma iniciativa estratégica em dezenas de itens de Product Backlog, redigir critérios de aceite em formato BDD impecáveis e preencher cerimônias com métricas aparentes de produtividade. Quadros do Jira e Miro, antes mantidos sob esforço analítico contínuo, agora são inflados em questão de segundos com centenas de "User Stories" perfeitamente formatadas. O mercado comemora essa agilidade operacional como um marco de produtividade sem precedentes. No entanto, essa percepção esconde um perigo silencioso: a aceleração do desperdício. Se o seu time acelerou dez vezes a capacidade de escrever, refinamento e entrega de itens de backlog sem validar se eles realmente resolvem problemas concretos de negócio ou de clientes, você não construiu uma operação de alta performance. Você apenas inaugurou a fábrica de features mais rápida e dispendiosa da história. O Paradoxo do Backlog Infinito e o Custo da Descoberta Falsa Historicamente, a lentidão para documentar e detalhar demandas funcionava, de forma não intencional, como um filtro de contenção. A restrição de tempo e capacidade cognitiva forçava o Product Owner a refletir: "Vale realmente a pena levar esta ideia adiante?" Hoje, a IA reduziu o custo marginal de geração de texto técnico a praticamente zero. O efeito colateral direto é o inchaço cognitivo e operacional : Falsa sensação de progresso: Confunde-se velocidade de documentação e taxa de throughput de tarefas com eficácia e geração de valor. Sobrecarga de refinamento: Times de desenvolvimento são soterrados por dezenas de histórias sintéticas cuja origem não é uma necessidade empírica real, mas a facilidade computacional de desdobrar listas infinitas. Diluição de foco: Quando tudo pode ser rapidamente documentado e justificado com prosa corporativa convincente gerada por modelos de linguagem, a capacidade de dizer "não" enfraquece. Como Ralph Jocham e Don McGreal enfatizam em The Professional Product Owner , o papel central do Product Owner nunca foi atuar como escrivão de requisitos ou administrador de backlog, mas como um tomador de risco focado em maximizar valor. Quando o PO terceiriza sua reflexão crítica e usa a IA apenas para produzir mais artefatos táticos, ele retrocede à postura de mero intermediário entre ideias não testadas e a esteira de desenvolvimento. A eficiência sem eficácia é a forma mais refinada de queimar caixa corporativo. O Antídoto Empírico: O Olhar do Evidence-Based Management (EBM) Para escapar da armadilha da eficiência sintética, a liderança de produtos precisa substituir métricas puramente operacionais (como velocidade do time ou volume de itens entregues) por uma governança orientada a evidências. É aqui que o framework de Evidence-Based Management (EBM) da Scrum.org se torna essencial na era da IA generativa. O EBM estrutura o valor em quatro Áreas de Valor-Chave (Key Value Areas - KVAs). Quando olhamos para a IA através dessa lente, o equilíbrio se reestabelece: 1.Current Value (CV) vs. Unrealized Value (UV) A IA frequentemente induz o time a otimizar o produto atual com funcionalidades secundárias que pouco alteram a receita ou a retenção. O papel do PO é usar IA não para inventar novas telas, mas para analisar dados reais de uso e suporte, identificando onde reside a maior oportunidade de valor ainda não realizado ( Unrealized Value ) com o menor esforço viável. 2. Time-to-Market (T2M) redefinido como Time-to-Learn Entregar código rápido não encerra o ciclo. Na gestão empírica, a velocidade que importa é o tempo que leva para uma hipótese sair da cabeça do time, encontrar um usuário real e retornar como evidência mensurável. A IA deve acelerar a construção de testes conceituais, simulações de fluxo e análise de feedback, encurtando o aprendizado — não apenas acelerando a esteira de deploy. 3. Ability to Innovate (A2I) Uma esteira entupida de features irrelevantes geradas por automação drena a capacidade de inovação do time. Quanto mais código periférico é enviado para produção sem validação de impacto, maior se torna o custo de sustentação, arquitetura e débito técnico, aniquilando a capacidade futura da organização de inovar. Da Geração de Features à Redução da Incerteza Se a inteligência artificial não deve ser usada para inflar o backlog, onde está o seu valor transformador para o Product Owner? A resposta reside em mudar o polo de atuação: da geração de artefatos de entrega para a qualificação da tomada de decisão . Abordagem Tradicional / Antipadroes VS Abordagem Pragmática com IA Geração linear: Pedir ao modelo para escrever histórias de usuário e critérios de aceite a partir de uma ideia abstrata. VS Desafio de hipóteses: Utilizar o modelo como sparring crítico para encontrar vieses, riscos de premissa e cenários de falha na tese de negócio. items.title: AI Generated the User Stories - Now the Real Work Begins
items.summary: AI can generate a list of user stories in seconds. The stories may be clearly written, correctly formatted and connected to recognisable user value. They can give a Product Owner and a whole Scrum Team something concrete to discuss without spending hours facing a blank page. This is genuinely useful – and it is where the more demanding work begins. A well-written user story can still contain an unsupported business rule, an unverified technical assumption or a product decision nobody has made. Once the output has been copied into the Product Backlog, shared with stakeholders or expanded into acceptance criteria, its origin becomes harder to see. A plausible suggestion starts to look like an agreed requirement. What concerns me most is not an obviously incorrect AI response, which is usually easier to notice and challenge. The greater risk is output that is mostly useful. It creates momentum, and momentum makes it tempting to continue working before asking which parts of the draft are supported by evidence. AI generates plausible material. It does not establish truth. Image llustration concept by Joanna Płaskonka, generated with AI The first draft is no longer the hardest part In my eBook, From Feature Idea to Sprint Planning , I explore this problem through VitaCare, a fictional healthcare organisation. Marta, its Product Owner, is working with a request to let patients book and reschedule appointments online without calling a clinic. AI can quickly turn this request into a structured patient journey and a collection of user stories: view eligible appointment types, find an available slot, review the details, confirm a booking, see the result and obtain assistance when self-service is unavailable. The result organises the experience around patient activities, connects the stories to value, includes failure and assisted routes, and avoids dividing the work into technical components. Yet closer inspection exposes questions the format does not answer. Some entries describe activities, some resemble user stories and others could become acceptance criteria. Several apparently separate stories form one dependent patient journey. A reference to choosing an “appropriate” appointment may imply clinical judgement, while viewing available slots depends on scheduling capabilities the team has not confirmed. Marta keeps the story map as a discovery artifact. She does not copy the entire output into the Product Backlog. AI has reduced the effort required to produce a first draft, but it has not created the shared understanding needed for responsible product decisions. Useful stories need an outcome to support The quality of Marta’s story map begins before she asks AI to generate it. The original feature request gives the team a direction, but it does not define which patients or appointments are included, how availability will be obtained, what happens when a selected slot is lost or when staff assistance is required. Even the word “book” hides multiple decisions. Marta’s first attempt at a Product Goal is: Launch online appointment booking this quarter. The sentence communicates an output and a timeframe. It does not describe the meaningful change the team wants to create. The feature could be launched while producing failed bookings, low adoption or additional clinic work. Marta asks AI to examine the goal, focus on outcomes and avoid inventing targets, policies or technical capabilities. The first response proposes: By the end of the quarter, enable eligible patients to book and reschedule supported appointments through MyVitaCare, reducing their need to call a clinic and providing immediate confirmation. This is an improvement. The response moves beyond delivery, connects patient and operational value, exposes missing scope and suggests useful indicators. It also avoids inventing a numerical target for reducing calls. Marta nevertheless does not accept the rewrite as a decision. “Immediate confirmation” assumes a capability the team has not validated. The quarterly deadline comes from the original statement, but no feasibility assessment has taken place. “Eligible” and “supported” sound careful while concealing decisions about patients, clinics and appointment types. Reduced call volume also requires interpretation. It could indicate successful self-service, but it could also mean that patients abandoned the process or stopped seeking assistance. An operational number is not sufficient evidence of a better patient outcome. After further review, Marta retains a provisional Product Goal: Enable eligible patients to independently book or reschedule supported appointments through MyVitaCare, giving them greater control and reducing avoidable clinic coordination while maintaining safe and reliable scheduling. She adds no deadline or numerical target yet. items.title: Ten Product Leaders, Ten Documents, No Strategy
items.summary: This is the first article in our AI Product Strategy Series. This article has been co-authored by Hamza El Uamari , Head of Product Decision Intelligence at KLM. Summary: Product strategy is the set of choices that explains how a product will win: who it serves, which needs it addresses, what makes it different, and how it creates value for the business. It connects product vision to the roadmap. A strong strategy requires a clear diagnosis and deliberate choices, not a feature list or a one-size-fits-all platform. In an AI-first environment, that discipline matters even more. AI expands what teams can build, but it does not decide what they should build. AI will not fix a weak strategy. It will expose it. Imagine asking ten product leaders to show you their product strategy. It’s likely you will receive ten very different documents in response. One will show you a vision statement. Another a roadmap. A third will show a list of features for the next two quarters. And someone will almost certainly have a slide with three pillars and a lot of arrows. Each may contain very relevant insights, context, or plans. But none of them actually showed you a product strategy. We see this repeatedly, and our intent is not to criticize product people. It is a symptom of how confused our profession still is about what a product strategy actually is. We talk about it frequently, but across the board, we’re still not very aligned on what it is and what it isn’t. In this ‘AI-First Product Strategy series, we will obviously explore how AI impacts product strategy. But before we do that, we first need to align on the concept. Many of the challenges product leaders will have with AI are problems they already had. AI will not fix a weak strategy. It will expose it. So, that’s where we need to start. Why ‘one size fits all’ is not a product strategy If you’ve been in product management for some time, you will have met companies and stakeholders who love the ‘one size fits all’ approach. It sounds responsible at first. It sounds efficient. It can even sound like good leadership to build one platform or product that serves everyone. Because our stakeholders love standardization, don’t they? But this particular flavor of ambition gets product leaders into trouble. In practice, such as combining three dashboards into one configurable dashboard because maintaining three feels wasteful, merging finance and operations tools because having two feels like duplication, or designing one feature to serve every persona because narrowing the audience feels like leaving value on the table. It rarely works because strategy is a set of choices, and choices mean saying no. Roman Pichler’s product strategy framework makes those choices explicit. He says: “a real product strategy requires you to pick a market, pick the needs you’ll address, pick what makes the product stand out, and pick the business goal it serves.” A product that tries to please everyone avoids those choices. It does not choose a market or prioritize a need. That is not strategy. It is the absence of a strategic product decision. Product strategy is more than a slide When people hear ‘product strategy,’ they often think of a slide, or multiple ones. Slides can absolutely help present your strategy to stakeholders, but the slide is not the strategy. Strategy has multiple layers, and there are different styles of strategy depending on the environment. Confusing those layers and styles is where a lot of the noise starts. The layers run from corporate strategy at the top, to business strategy beneath it, to product strategy, alongside supporting strategies like go-to-market, pricing, marketing, sales, and technology strategy. Knowing which layer you’re operating at prevents a lot of pointless meetings where people argue past each other because they’re solving problems at different altitudes. In ‘Your Strategy Needs a Strategy’ Reeves, Haanaes, and Sinha argue that the right approach to styles depends on your environment. How predictable it is, how much you can shape it, and how harsh it is, all influence the strategy style. They describe five approaches, called the ‘Strategy Palette’: Classical (be big): win through position and scale in a stable, predictable market. Adaptive (be fast): win through constant experimentation when the environment shifts quickly. Visionary (be first): create or recreate a market you can see coming and pursue it single-mindedly. Shaping (be the orchestrator): influence an emerging market by coordinating with other players. Renewal (be viable): restore strength first when the environment has turned harsh. Figure 1: The Strategy Palette, by BCG These styles matter because the right strategy depends on the environment. A scale-first approach may work in a stable market, but it can be costly in an environment that requires an Adaptive or Visionary style. AI-first markets make this mismatch especially visible.…

items.summary: In Thailand sind Fossilien einer bisher unbekannten urzeitlichen „Riesenratte“ entdeckt worden. Das schätzungsweise 30 Kilogramm schwere Nagetier lebte laut einer Studie im Paläogen vor 33 bis 35 Millionen Jahren.

items.title: Jeder vierte Jugendliche bewegt sich kaum
items.summary: Eine Stunde Bewegung pro Tag empfiehlt die Weltgesundheitsorganisation (WHO) für Jugendliche. Wie ein neuer Bericht zeigt, kommen dem aber nur wenige nach. Jeder vierte Jugendliche ist körperlich sogar gar nicht aktiv.

items.title: Dauerstress beeinflusst Vertrauen
items.summary: Menschen, die darüber berichten, in ihrem Leben über längere Zeit erhöhtem Stress ausgesetzt gewesen zu sein, haben weniger Vertrauen in andere Menschen. Das ergab eine neue Studie.

items.title: Auch Katzen können schüchtern sein
items.summary: Wenn Katzen Fremden aus dem Weg gehen, wird das oft als Ängstlichkeit abgetan. Warum das ihrer komplexen Persönlichkeit überhaupt nicht gerecht wird, zeigt eine neue Studie. Laut dieser sind manche Katzen schlicht schüchtern – ähnlich wie menschliche Babys.

items.title: NASA-Satellit auf Erde gestürzt
items.summary: Nach dem Scheitern einer beispiellosen Rettungsmission der US-Raumfahrtbehörde NASA ist ein Forschungssatellit auf die Erde gestürzt. Der Satellit sei ungefähr über Indonesien wieder in die Erdatmosphäre eingetreten, teilte die NASA mit.

items.title: Messung der KI-Wirksamkeit: Was Ihr Velocity-Chart dem CFO nicht sagen kann 🇩🇪
items.summary: In Kürze: KI-Wirksamkeit auf Teamebene messen Früher oder später zeigt jemand in Ihrer Organisation eine Folie mit einer Zahl dazu, was KI für Ihr Team bewirkt hat: typischerweise die „Velocity“ des Teams vor und nach der Einführung der Coding-Agenten, dazu ein Prozentsatz, der wie eine Rendite auf die Token-Rechnung aussieht. Die Zahl mag sogar „stimmen“, beantwortet jedoch eine andere Frage als die, die die Finanzabteilung stellt: Ein Vorher-nachher-Vergleich schreibt jede Veränderung in diesem Zeitraum den KI-Agenten gut, und die Sinnhaftigkeit der Velocity ist unter normalen Umständen aus gutem Grund umstritten, was die Messung der KI-Wirksamkeit auf diesem Weg noch schwieriger macht. Eine Aussage, die Ihr Team vertreten kann, beginnt woanders: mit einer ehrlichen Einstufung der Belege, einem Break-even-Test für jeden an KI delegierten Workflow und der Creep-Prüfung (schleichende Kategorienverschiebung von „Assist“ zu „Automate“) des KI-Delegations-Audits, die diejenigen Workflows aufspürt, die den Test nur bestehen, weil niemand ihren Output mehr prüft. Jeder Workflow erhält anschließend im datierten Auditprotokoll eine Entscheidung: behalten, ändern oder ausmustern. Das Ergebnis passt auf eine Seite, die festhält, was das Team behaupten kann und was nicht. Bonus: Ein kleiner Versuch mit acht bis zehn Durchläufen liefert eine Einschätzung zur Messung der KI-Wirksamkeit für Ihre eigene Arbeit. 📺 Watch the article’s video : Measuring AI Impact: What Your Velocity Chart Cannot Tell the CFO . Image Thesis : Dieser Artikel erklärt, wie agile Teams die KI-Wirksamkeit wirksam messen, warum Velocity-Charts im Vorher-nachher-Vergleich in die Irre führen, welche drei Stufen von Belegen es gibt, wie der Break-even-Test für delegierte Workflows funktioniert, was eine einseitige Stellungnahme für die Finanzabteilung enthält und wie Sie einen persönlichen Versuch zur Messung der KI-Wirksamkeit Ihrer persönlichen Arbeit durchführen. Transparenzhinweis : Ich habe das Buch von Charniak und McDermott über „Artificial Intelligence“ vor Jahrzehnten gelesen; selbstverständlich nutze ich KI für Recherche, Übersetzungen, Korrekturlesen, das Hinterfragen von Spannungsbögen und Artikelstrukturen, die Erstellung von Artefakten wie Grafiken sowie für Zusammenfassungen. KI ist ein Produktionswerkzeug, kein Ersatz für das Denken. 🗞 Shall I notify you about articles like this one? Awesome! You can sign up here for the ‘Food for Agile Thought’ newsletter and join 35,000-plus subscribers . 🎓 Nehmen Sie an einer meiner kommenden Schulungen zu den Themen KI, Scrum, Produktmanagement oder Agile teil ! Die Frage des CFO ist berechtigt Lassen Sie mich raten: Die Zahl kam früher an als die Frage. In einem All-Hands, einem Lenkungskreis mit Stakeholdern oder einem Quartalsbericht zeigte eine Folie die Velocity des Teams in den Monaten vor der KI-Einführung neben den Monaten danach, mit einem grünen Pfeil und einem Prozentsatz, und niemand im Raum fragte, was in diesen Monaten sonst noch geschehen war. Der Prozentsatz wanderte anschließend nach oben in die nächste Präsentation für das Board. Einige Wochen später stellt die Finanzabteilung die Frage, die die Folie scheinbar beantwortete: Was bringen uns die Ausgaben für KI, und woran würden wir das erkennen? Die Frage ist berechtigt, zumal viele Führungskräfte „Velocity“ trotz der Kontroverse weiterhin als sinnvolles Maß für die Produktivität eines Teams ansehen, manchmal sogar als Maß für den Fortschritt. Das Velocity-Chart sieht wie die naheliegende Antwort auf die Anfrage des CFO aus, kann jedoch nicht leisten, was die Finanzabteilung von ihm erwartet. Warum ein Vorher-nachher-Chart alles den Agenten gutschreibt Teams verändern selten nur eine Sache auf einmal. Die Coding-Agenten treffen im selben Quartal auf einen neuen Sprint-Rhythmus, das Ausscheiden eines Teammitglieds, eine Reorganisation, ein großes Release oder ein neues Produktziel beziehungsweise ein neues Ziel der Produkt-Roadmap. Der Vergleich von „vorher“ mit „nachher“ schreibt all das den Agenten zu. Auch das „Vorher“ muss keine stabile Ausgangsbasis sein: Folgte die Einführung auf eine Crunch-Phase oder hatten Teammitglieder KI schon lange vor den offiziellen Lizenzen privat genutzt, misst der Vergleich auch diese Phase und die private Nutzung von Shadow-IT mit. James Shore, der im September 2026 eine Artikelserie über die Messung der KI-Wirksamkeit veröffentlicht hat, benennt das Problem in Measuring AI’s Impact on Delivery Speed : „Gehen Ihre Geschwindigkeitszuwächse auf die Einführung von KI zurück? Oder auf die anderen Änderungen, die Sie gleichzeitig vorgenommen haben?“ Seine Abhilfe besteht darin, Aufgaben „ohne KI“ und „mit KI“ im selben Zeitraum „zu verschränken“, was „den Einfluss anderer Änderungen verringert“. Das ist ein Studiendesign, und ein Studiendesign erfordert eine Entscheidung, bevor die Arbeit beginnt, weshalb ein nachträglich zusammengestelltes Chart dies nicht ersetzen kann. Die Frage an jede…

items.title: Vulkanische Aktivität auf Mars möglich
items.summary: Eine neue Studie legt nahe, dass der Mars im Inneren geologisch gesehen keineswegs tot ist. Unter der Oberfläche des Planeten könnte eine schlafende Magmakammer liegen, so das Forschungsteam.

items.title: NASA is racing against time to save the Hubble Space Telescope
items.summary: NASA is exploring a daring plan to save the legendary Hubble Space Telescope from its eventual fiery plunge into Earth's atmosphere. After more than 35 years of groundbreaking discoveries, Hubble is slowly losing altitude, and without intervention, it could fall back to Earth as early as 2033 or 2034. To keep the iconic observatory operating, NASA is asking private space companies to propose innovative ways to boost Hubble into a higher orbit, upgrade its capabilities, or safely dispose of it when its mission finally ends.

items.title: AI helps Stanford scientists discover a “natural Ozempic” with a surprising advantage
items.summary: Stanford researchers have discovered an AI-identified natural molecule that dramatically suppresses appetite and promotes fat loss in animals, potentially offering an Ozempic-like weight-loss treatment without common digestive side effects or significant muscle loss. Called BRP, the molecule reduced food intake by up to 50% and targets a different brain pathway, raising hopes for a more precise obesity treatment if future human trials prove successful.

items.title: A hidden star is plowing through Betelgeuse’s atmosphere, new evidence suggests
items.summary: Something mysterious is disturbing Betelgeuse, and astronomers believe they have identified the culprit: a hidden companion star called Siwarha. New radio observations reveal that the smaller star may be plowing through Betelgeuse’s enormous atmosphere, creating disturbances that subtly stretch and distort the red supergiant’s shape.

items.title: Kids who eat more ultra-processed foods show a troubling brain response
items.summary: A new study suggests that ultra-processed foods may influence children's developing brains in ways that encourage weight gain. Researchers from USC studied 46 children ages 7 to 10 and found that those who ate more ultra-processed foods showed stronger activity in the brain's reward system when viewing tempting foods like cookies and French fries. These heightened brain responses were linked to greater increases in body fat and body mass index (BMI) one year later, suggesting that the brain's sensitivity to food cues may help explain why ultra-processed diets are associated with obesity.

items.title: Wissenschaftler entdecken überraschende Vorteile für das Herz, wenn man jeden Tag Avocado und Mango isst
items.summary: Laut einer neuen Studie mit Erwachsenen mit Prädiabetes kann der tägliche Verzehr einer Avocado und einer Tasse Mango überraschende Vorteile für die Herzgesundheit haben. Bereits nach acht Wochen stellten die Teilnehmer vor allem bei Männern deutliche Verbesserungen der Blutgefäßfunktion und des diastolischen Blutdrucks fest. Diese Vorteile traten ohne Gewichtszunahme oder Veränderungen der Kalorienaufnahme auf, was darauf hindeutet, dass die nährstoffreiche Kombination die Herz-Kreislauf-Gesundheit durch eine einfache Ernährungsumstellung unterstützen könnte.
items.origTitle: Scientists discover surprising heart benefits of eating avocado and mango every day
items.origSummary: Eating an avocado and a cup of mango every day may provide surprising benefits for heart health, according to a new study involving adults with prediabetes. After just eight weeks, participants experienced significant improvements in blood vessel function and diastolic blood pressure, particularly among men. These benefits occurred without weight gain or changes in calorie intake, suggesting that the nutrient-rich combination could support cardiovascular health through a simple dietary adjustment.

items.title: Alle 5 genetischen „Buchstaben“ von DNA und RNA in einem 4,5 Milliarden Jahre alten Asteroiden entdeckt
items.summary: Wissenschaftler haben alle fünf essentiellen Nukleobasen, die in DNA und RNA verwendet werden, in unberührten Proben des Asteroiden Ryugu entdeckt und damit gezeigt, dass es vor Milliarden von Jahren im Weltraum Schlüsselbestandteile für Leben gab. Der bemerkenswerte Befund ergänzt die zunehmenden Beweise anderer Asteroiden und Meteoriten, dass diese Moleküle im gesamten frühen Sonnensystem weit verbreitet waren.
items.origTitle: All 5 genetic “letters” of DNA and RNA discovered in a 4.5-billion-year-old asteroid
items.origSummary: Scientists have discovered all five essential nucleobases used in DNA and RNA in pristine samples from asteroid Ryugu, revealing that key ingredients for life existed in space billions of years ago. The remarkable finding adds to growing evidence from other asteroids and meteorites that these molecules were widespread throughout the early Solar System.

items.title: Die NASA prallte gegen einen Asteroiden. Jetzt kommt Hera näher, um zu sehen, was passiert ist
items.summary: Die europäische Raumsonde Hera hat ihre erste klare Sicht auf zwei Asteroiden aufgenommen, die an dem historischen Experiment der NASA im Jahr 2022 zur Umlenkung eines potenziell gefährlichen Weltraumgesteins beteiligt waren. Während sie sich nun dem Paar nähert, wird Hera die mysteriösen Folgen der Kollision untersuchen und herausfinden, warum sich der Asteroid weitaus stärker verschoben hat, als die Wissenschaftler vorhergesagt hatten.
items.origTitle: NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera is closing in to see what happened
items.origSummary: Europe’s Hera spacecraft has captured its first clear view of two asteroids involved in NASA’s historic 2022 experiment to redirect a potentially dangerous space rock. Now approaching the pair, Hera will investigate the mysterious aftermath of the collision and uncover why the asteroid shifted far more than scientists predicted.

items.title: Die Voyager 1 der NASA steht kurz davor, einen historischen Ein-Licht-Tag-Meilenstein zu erreichen
items.summary: Die Voyager 1 der NASA nähert sich fast 50 Jahre nach ihrem Start einem außergewöhnlichen Meilenstein, obwohl die Ingenieure mit schwindender Leistung und mysteriösen technischen Problemen zu kämpfen haben. Ein cleveres Energiesparmanöver hat die wissenschaftliche Mission der Raumsonde verlängert, während ein ungeklärter 48-stündiger Kommunikationsausfall der NASA kürzlich Angst einjagte. Am 18. November wird Voyager 1 eine Entfernung von einem Lichttag von der Erde erreichen, sodass selbst die einfachste Hin- und Rückkommunikation 48 Stunden dauern würde.
items.origTitle: NASA’s Voyager 1 is about to reach a historic one-light-day milestone
items.origSummary: NASA’s Voyager 1 is approaching an extraordinary milestone nearly 50 years after its launch, even as engineers battle dwindling power and mysterious technical problems. A clever energy-saving maneuver has extended the spacecraft’s scientific mission, while an unexplained 48-hour communications blackout recently gave NASA a scare. On November 18, Voyager 1 will reach a distance of one light-day from Earth, making even the simplest round-trip communication take 48 hours.

items.title: Wissenschaftler entdecken neues Alzheimer-Medikament, das DNA-Schäden repariert und Gehirnentzündungen reduziert
items.summary: Wissenschaftler haben herausgefunden, dass ein Medikament, das ursprünglich für Rückenmarksverletzungen entwickelt wurde, mehrere Hauptmerkmale der Alzheimer-Krankheit bekämpfen kann, darunter DNA-Schäden und Entzündungen. Die experimentelle Behandlung wurde bereits auf anfängliche Sicherheit beim Menschen getestet und könnte einen schnelleren Weg zu Therapien bieten, die die Krankheit an ihren Wurzeln ansetzen.
items.origTitle: Scientists discover new Alzheimer’s drug that repairs DNA damage and reduces brain inflammation
items.origSummary: Scientists have discovered that a drug originally developed for spinal cord injuries can tackle several key features of Alzheimer’s disease, including DNA damage and inflammation. Already tested for initial safety in humans, the experimental treatment could offer a faster path toward therapies that target the disease at its roots.

items.title: Wissenschaftler haben gerade ein Schlupfloch gefunden, das dazu führen könnte, dass Schwarze Löcher in zwei Teile geteilt werden
items.summary: Wissenschaftler haben eine mögliche Lücke in den Gesetzen entdeckt, die normalerweise verhindern, dass Schwarze Löcher auseinanderbrechen, was darauf hindeutet, dass sich extrem schnell rotierende Schwarze Löcher in zwei Teile teilen könnten. Der überraschende Befund lässt die Möglichkeit eines völlig neuen Schwarzlochphänomens aufkommen, das künftige Teleskope möglicherweise entdecken könnten.
items.origTitle: Scientists just found a loophole that could let black holes split in two
items.origSummary: Scientists have discovered a possible loophole in the laws that normally prevent black holes from splitting apart, suggesting that extremely fast-spinning black holes might divide into two. The surprising finding raises the possibility of an entirely new black hole phenomenon that future telescopes could potentially detect.
